KEY MESSAGE 1...

Lingering showers and storms will continue to move through the 
region early this morning. As they exit the region, a shortwave 
approaches the region. This shortwave will support another round of 
showers and thunderstorms today, mainly this afternoon and evening. 
Models are showing anywhere from 500 to 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE this 
afternoon, though shear will be weak ranging from 20 to 30 kts. Mid-
level lapse rates will generally be low across the region though 
there will be some pockets of modest values. While these values are 
not too impressive, there will likely be enough of these ingredients 
to support a few stronger storms today. The greatest hazard would be 
strong winds, given the higher DCAPE values seen in forecast 
soundings and slightly stronger flow above the surface that could 
mix down. Instability extends into the hail growth zone as well, so 
small hail may be possible. As of now, the greatest potential for 
strong to severe storms is over the Wyoming Valley and areas south 
of the region. If some clearing can take place, then areas further 
north could also see isolated stronger storms.

Looking at moisture for today, PWATs will be 1.5 to 1.75 inches. 
While not particularly high, there is potential for quasi-stationary 
storm motions. Given this, locally heavy rainfall will be possible 
and could lead to localized flash flooding. Areas that were hit 
hardest yesterday would be more sensitive to higher rainfall
amounts.

When it is not raining, it will be warm and humid. Temperatures will 
max out in the 80s with dew points in the upper 60s to low 70s. Heat 
index values will be around or exceed 90 in the valleys, but
stay below heat advisory criteria.

Overnight, a weak cold front will begin to pass through. This may 
support a few additional rain showers, but these will be lighter. 
With the added moisture and winds calming, fog will develop, 
especially in the valleys. Temperatures stay fairly mild, only 
dropping into the 60s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...

While there will not be much of a cool down on tomorrow, drier air 
moves in and significantly decreases the humidity. Surface high 
pressure will bring a quiet end to the weekend. Monday will also 
start out dry but rain is quick to move in with the next 
disturbance. Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected Monday 
afternoon and evening. There will be enhanced mid-level flow, which 
equates to higher shear. The low level flow will also be 
stronger than seen this weekend. There is still some uncertainty
on how much instability will develop. PWATs will be enhanced 
with values of at least 1.75 inches. While there are still 
uncertainties if all ingredients come together, Monday will be 
the next day to monitor for the potential for strong storms and 
heavy rainfall.

The general pattern will keep a broad trough over the region the 
rest of the week. Multiple shortwaves will move through during this 
time and support off-and-on scattered showers Tuesday through 
Thursday. During this stretch, moisture may become limited on 
Wednesday, so there will be potential for a brief dry period for 
most, if not all of the region. One more system looks to push 
through near the end of the week before high pressure returns just 
before the weekend.

After a warm start, temperatures will trend cooler throughout 
the week and be closer to or even slightly below normal.
